report.body:
## TL;DR

The Pharmacare Act, assented to on 10 October 2024, is an enabling framework rather than a program: it creates a conditional federal spending power over contraception and diabetes products only, requires first-dollar coverage in any agreement, and delivers that coverage through existing provincial plans with no application process for residents [1][2][3]. It names no drug, sets no formulary, contains no dollar figure, and requires no province to participate, so coverage exists only where a bilateral agreement has been signed [1]. That makes the map of signed agreements, the covered lists and the claims data the real measures of delivery — and this report does not establish any of the three, because no Health Canada, PBO, CIHI or provincial document could be retrieved for it. The cost question in particular is left with a method rather than a number.

## Key Findings

- The Pharmacare Act (Bill C-64) received royal assent on 10 October 2024 and became chapter 24 of the 2024 Statutes of Canada [1].
- Its purpose clause commits only to guiding efforts toward national universal pharmacare, "with the aim of continuing to work toward the implementation of national universal pharmacare" — it does not implement it [1].
- Federal payments require an agreement with a province or territory; without one, no money flows and no coverage exists, which makes participation voluntary and the agreement list the measure of delivery [1].
- The spending power is confined to "specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes" — there is no statutory drug list, and the item-level list is set outside the Act [1][3].
- The Act requires first-dollar coverage in every agreement, meaning no deductible or co-payment at the counter for covered items, and specifies delivery through existing provincial plans rather than a new federal plan [3].
- Eligibility is automatic for residents of participating jurisdictions who qualify for their provincial health plan, and the Canadian Medical Association states there is no application process — so no enrolment count exists to cite [2].
- Automatic eligibility is not the same as automatic reimbursement: some diabetes drugs, including saxagliptin and metformin, are not automatically covered but are available with special authorization from the patient's health team [2].
- The Act commits the government to long-term funding beginning with rare diseases, primarily through agreements with provinces and territories, and names no amount — so every dollar figure in circulation is an estimate of a program the Act authorises but does not fund at a stated amount [1].
- Three deliverables fell due on 10 October 2025: the Canadian Drug Agency's essential medicines list, a pan-Canadian appropriate-use strategy, and an expert committee report on options for operation and financing that must be tabled in Parliament [1]. Their delivery status is not established here.
- This report does not establish which provinces and territories have signed, what the per-jurisdiction dollar amounts are, how many claims have been paid, or what the PBO and other independent estimates put the full program's cost at. Searches returned service errors and no primary document on any of those points was read; the cost section sets out the six assumptions that make estimates diverge instead of reporting figures.

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act (2024) actually committed Canada to — the statutory content, the timelines, and what is and is not yet in force

The statute at the centre of this question is Bill C-64, the Pharmacare Act, which received royal assent on 10 October 2024 and became chapter 24 of the 2024 Statutes of Canada [1]. Reading it is the necessary starting point, because almost every claim made about "national pharmacare" in Canada since then — that it exists, that it covers something, that it is or is not funded — depends on what this text does and does not authorise. The short answer from the text itself is that the Act is an enabling framework, not a program. It creates no benefit, names no drug, and appropriates no sum of money. Everything that has actually reached a pharmacy counter has reached it through a separate bilateral agreement with a province or territory, which is why the questions of which governments signed and what is covered are not administrative details but the whole substance of the policy.

The purpose clause is unusually modest for a piece of legislation that was sold politically as the foundation of universal pharmacare. Section 3 states that the purpose is "to guide efforts to improve, for all Canadians, the accessibility and affordability of prescription drugs and related products," in collaboration with provinces, territories, Indigenous peoples and other partners, "with the aim of continuing to work toward the implementation of national universal pharmacare" [1]. The operative verb is "guide"; the object is "efforts"; and the endpoint is something the Act describes as still to be implemented, not something it implements. A reader looking for a statutory entitlement to prescription drug coverage will not find one here.

What the Act does contain is a single, tightly conditional spending power. Section 6(1) provides that the Minister must make payments to a province or territory only "if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so," and the purpose of those payments is defined narrowly: to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage and to provide "universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage" for "specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes" [1]. Three features of that sentence do most of the work in explaining the program's actual footprint. First, the obligation is triggered by an agreement — no agreement, no payment, no coverage, which makes the map of signed deals the real measure of delivery. Second, the subject matter is confined to two clinical categories, contraception and diabetes; the Act does not create authority to fund anything else. Third, the coverage standard is prescribed in law rather than left to negotiation: section 6 goes on to specify, "For greater certainty, any agreement referred to in subsection (1) with a province or territory is to provide for first-dollar coverage to patients" [3]. First-dollar means no deductible and no co-payment charged to the patient at the point of dispensing for the covered items — the plan pays from the first dollar of the prescription's cost. That is a materially stronger standard than most existing provincial plans meet for working-age adults, and it is the reason the agreements have been presented as an improvement to existing coverage rather than a top-up.

The phrase "related products" in section 6(1) is what allows the diabetes side of the program to include devices and supplies rather than only molecules [1]. That is an inference from the statutory wording rather than something the Act spells out, but it matters for what follows, because the diabetes category is where the covered list runs well beyond tablets and insulin.

The Act's other obligations are process obligations with deadlines, and they are worth listing because their due dates have now passed and their completion is checkable independently of any agreement. Section 8(1) required the Minister, after discussions with the provinces and territories, to request that the Canadian Drug Agency prepare — "no later than the first anniversary of the day on which this Act receives royal assent" — a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that would "establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare" [1]. Section 10(1) required a pan-Canadian strategy on the appropriate use of prescription drugs, published on Health Canada's website, by the same anniversary [1]. Section 11(1) required the Minister to establish a committee of experts within 30 days of royal assent, with a mandate to "make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare" [1]. Given royal assent on 10 October 2024, the committee was due by roughly 9 November 2024, and the essential medicines list, the appropriate-use strategy and the committee's report were all due by 10 October 2025 — arithmetic on the Act's own text rather than a separate source.

None of these three deliverables creates coverage. They are the scaffolding for a program that the Act contemplates but does not constitute, and the distinction is the one that gets lost in public argument. A published essential medicines list would define what a future universal plan ought to cover; it would not entitle anyone to a drug. The committee's report would describe financing options; it would not finance anything.

Finally, section 5 sets out the funding posture in deliberately non-numeric terms: the Government of Canada commits to maintaining long-term funding for the provinces, territories and Indigenous peoples to improve the accessibility and affordability of pharmaceutical products, beginning with those for rare diseases, and specifies that funding for provinces and territories "must be provided primarily through agreements with their respective governments" [1]. Two things follow from that wording. The commitment is sequenced — it begins with rare diseases, not with the contraception and diabetes coverage that section 6 funds — and it is channelled through agreements, the same instrument that gates section 6. There is no dollar figure anywhere in the Act. Any number attached to national pharmacare, in either the government's announcements or the Parliamentary Budget Officer's costing, is therefore an estimate of a program that legislation has authorised but not funded at a stated amount.

Read as a whole, the Act's structure explains the shape of the public record since October 2024. Because coverage requires a named bilateral agreement, delivery is uneven by construction and varies with provincial politics rather than with federal entitlement. Because the eligible categories are fixed at contraception and diabetes, the program's reach is small relative to total prescription spending, whatever the eventual cost of a full universal plan turns out to be. And because the Act contains deadlines for lists, strategies and reports but no deadline for signing agreements with any particular province, the pace of the rollout is not something the statute controls. The questions that follow — who signed, what is covered, who is using it, what a full program would cost — are all questions about matters the Act left open.

### 2. Which provinces and territories have signed bilateral agreements with Ottawa, on what terms and for how much money, and who has not signed

This section reports a gap, and it is a gap of retrieval rather than of public evidence: the agreements exist, Health Canada publishes them, and provincial governments announce their own. This report did not reach those documents, so what follows is not a finding that nothing is documented.

What the record does establish is the structure the question turns on. Under section 6(1) of the Pharmacare Act, federal money reaches a patient only if the Minister has entered into an agreement with that patient's province or territory, and only for the purpose of increasing existing public coverage of contraception and diabetes products [1]. No agreement means no payment and no coverage. The map of signed bilateral agreements is therefore not a progress indicator on some larger program; it is the program. The Act itself contains no covered list: it describes the categories and leaves the item-level list to be set elsewhere, in the agreements and in federal guidance [3]. A national account of what is covered and who is using it therefore has to be assembled jurisdiction by jurisdiction rather than read off the statute.

Beyond that, the specific facts this section was meant to establish — which provinces and territories have signed, on what dates, for what per-jurisdiction dollar amounts, and which governments have declined or not yet concluded an agreement — are not in this report. Every search run for this question returned a service error, and the federal pharmacare pages could not be retrieved, so no primary or credible secondary source on the agreement list was read, and recalled figures were not substituted for checked ones. The consequence is that a reader of this section learns how the program is gated but not where it is operating. The answer lives in documents that are public: Health Canada publishes the bilateral agreements and their terms, provincial governments announce their own, and the agreement texts set the covered lists. A revised version of this report should build this section from those documents, with the signing date, the federal contribution, the covered products and the effective date for each jurisdiction in a table, and should treat any province that has not signed as a substantive finding rather than an omission, since the Act's design leaves participation voluntary.

Two points follow from the structure, and the first holds regardless of which jurisdictions have signed. First, the pace of the rollout is not something the statute controls: the Act sets deadlines for a national formulary list, an appropriate-use strategy and an expert committee report, but sets no deadline for concluding an agreement with any particular province [1]. Delivery therefore tracks federal-provincial politics rather than a legislative timetable. Second, because eligibility runs through the provincial or territorial health plan rather than through a federal entitlement, a resident must both live in a jurisdiction that has signed and qualify for that jurisdiction's health plan to be covered [2]; and where no agreement exists, the payments in section 6(1) cannot flow at all [1]. The Canadian Medical Association's explainer, which lists Prince Edward Island among participating jurisdictions, sets eligibility out in exactly those terms [2]. Coverage of the same contraceptive or diabetes product is therefore a function of jurisdiction, which is the substantive cost of a voluntary design, and it is the thing to measure once the agreement list is in hand.

### 3. What is actually covered: the contraception and diabetes drugs and devices list, who is eligible, and how coverage is delivered in practice

The scope of what is covered is set by statute only at the level of a category, not a list. Section 6(1) authorises federal payments to a province or territory "in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes" [3]. The Act names no drug, no device and no product identifier. The covered list is therefore established outside the statute, in the bilateral agreements and in the federal guidance that accompanies them, and the statutory text fixes only the two clinical purposes the spending must serve.

That drafting choice has a practical consequence worth stating plainly: anyone asking "is my prescription covered" cannot answer it from the Act. The Act tells you the categories — contraception, and treatment of diabetes — and the coverage standard, but the item-level detail lives in instruments that are not legislation and that can differ in emphasis from agreement to agreement. It also means the Act's scope can only be widened by amending it or by renegotiating agreements, not by administrative decision.

The coverage standard is, however, specified in law and is the most consequential thing in the Act for patients. The Act provides, "For greater certainty, any agreement referred to in subsection (1) with a province or territory is to provide for first-dollar coverage to patients" [3]. First-dollar coverage means the plan pays from the first dollar of the cost of a covered prescription: no deductible to satisfy and no co-payment collected at the pharmacy counter for those items. Because the standard is written into the Act rather than left to negotiation, it applies to every agreement that is concluded.

The words "related products" in section 6(1) are broad enough to be worth noting [3]. The Act's spending power is over specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes, not over drugs alone, which leaves room for the agreements to fund non-drug items in the diabetes category. Whether they in fact do is a question for the agreement texts, which this report did not reach.

The delivery architecture is also fixed in law, and it is the reason eligibility mechanics differ across the country. The Act does not create a federal plan with a federal card. Section 6(1) contemplates payments to a province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage, which places the provincial and territorial public plans — not a new federal insurer — as the paying entity [3]. Coverage is delivered through the plan a resident already has or is entitled to. This is a deliberate design choice consistent with the jurisdiction provinces hold over health care delivery, and it explains why the program is described in federal communications as a series of agreements rather than as a single benefit.

For the patient, the most important feature of that design is that there is no federal application to complete — though, as noted below, the covered list is not uniformly automatic at the counter. The Canadian Medical Association's explainer states that residents of the participating provinces and territories who qualify for their provincial health care plan are eligible, and that "There's no application process" [2]. Eligibility is automatic by residence and by membership in the provincial health plan; there is no federal enrolment form, no income test described in the Act, and no separate card. Two things follow. The first is administrative simplicity for patients: a covered contraceptive or diabetes product dispensed to an eligible resident in a participating province should be billed at zero to the patient without the patient having done anything to become eligible. The second is a measurement problem that shapes the next section. Because eligibility follows the provincial health plan, there is no federal application and no federal beneficiary file to count; the record of who is covered sits with the provincial plan, and usage has to be read from claims and dispensing rather than from a federal register [2].

What the Act does not do is equally worth stating. It does not require any province or territory to participate. It does not set a national formulary — section 8(1) only asks the Canadian Drug Agency to prepare a list of essential prescription drugs to inform the development of a national formulary, which is a later and separate step [1]. Its section 6 spending power is confined to contraception and diabetes products, so it creates no federal entitlement to coverage of a prescription outside those categories. The Act does, however, contemplate federal money outside them: section 5 commits the government to long-term funding to improve the accessibility and affordability of pharmaceutical products, beginning with those for rare diseases, though it names no amount [1]. That is a funding commitment rather than a benefit, and it sits on a separate track from the section 6 payments.

There is one material qualification to the automatic-coverage picture, and it comes from the same explainer. Not every product inside the covered categories is reimbursed without paperwork: some drugs in the diabetes category, including saxagliptin and metformin, are not automatically covered but are available with special authorization, which requires the patient's health team to submit an application [2]. Automatic eligibility for the program and automatic reimbursement of every covered product are therefore not the same thing, and the special-authorization step is where the two part company.

The practical result is a program whose covered perimeter is narrow and whose depth within that perimeter is generous. For a resident of a participating province filling a prescription for a contraceptive or an automatically covered diabetes product, the intended experience is a zero balance at the counter. For a resident of a non-participating province, or for a resident of any province filling a prescription outside those two categories, the Act changes nothing. Both halves of that sentence are consequences of the same statutory design, and the second half is the one that tends to be omitted when the Act is described as national pharmacare.

One limit on this section should be recorded. The specific drugs and devices on the covered lists, and any differences between agreements, are not established by the statutory text I have read, and I was not able to reach the federal program pages that would set them out. What the law establishes — the two categories, the first-dollar standard, delivery through existing provincial plans, automatic eligibility, no application — is documented above. The item-level list is not, and a reader who needs it should consult Health Canada's pharmacare pages and the individual bilateral agreements rather than rely on this section.

### 4. How many people are actually using it — enrolment, claims and dispensing figures, and what they do and do not show

This is the hardest of the five questions to answer with evidence, and the difficulty is structural rather than a gap in reporting. Because eligibility for the program is automatic, there is no register of participants to count. The Canadian Medical Association's explainer on how pharmacare works states that residents of the participating provinces and territories who also qualify for their provincial health care plan are eligible, and adds, "There's no application process" [2]. Nobody signs up. A resident of a participating province becomes a covered person by virtue of residence and provincial health plan membership, whether or not they ever fill a prescription for a contraceptive or a diabetes product.

The consequence for measurement is direct: any number presented as pharmacare "enrolment" is not an enrolment figure in the sense that the Canada Dental Care Plan or the Canada Child Benefit has enrolment. There is no federal application, no federal file of beneficiaries, and therefore no federal count of people who have "joined." Usage can only be observed downstream, at the point of dispensing, through claims paid by the provincial plans under the bilateral agreements. That means the available measures are of two kinds, and they answer different questions. Claim and dispensing counts tell you how many prescriptions were filled at zero cost to the patient under the agreement's terms. They do not tell you how many people were eligible, how many people had a clinical need for a covered product, or how many people obtained a covered product but were billed for it because of an administrative or listing gap.

Three further problems limit what any usage figure can show, and they follow from the program's design rather than from any particular data release. First, the counterfactual is invisible. The statutory purpose of the payments is to increase existing public coverage [3], and in at least one participating province the design extends coverage to people who had none: the Canadian Medical Association describes Manitoba's program as covering birth control and diabetes medications for residents not already covered through other public drug programs [2]. Where an agreement upgrades an existing benefit, a claim count measures a change in who paid rather than a change in whether the prescription happened; where it extends coverage to the previously uninsured, it measures something closer to new access. The two cannot be separated from a claim total alone. Without a comparison of dispensing volumes before and after an agreement took effect, a rising count is compatible both with more people obtaining contraceptives and diabetes products and with the same people obtaining the same products with a different payer. Distinguishing them requires before-and-after dispensing analysis of the kind provincial drug plan administrators are positioned to do.

Second, coverage starts on different dates in different jurisdictions, because each agreement has its own effective date. A national total at any given moment aggregates provinces at different points in their rollout, and a total that rises over time may be reflecting nothing more than a new province coming on stream rather than increased use within provinces already participating. Any usage figure needs its date and its list of participating jurisdictions attached to be interpretable.

Third, automatic eligibility makes the denominator the eligible population rather than the participating population, but eligibility carries two conditions: residence in a participating jurisdiction and qualification for that jurisdiction's health plan [2]. The CMA explainer also records that some drugs inside the diabetes category, including saxagliptin and metformin, are not automatically covered but are available with special authorization [2]. The interesting rate is therefore not what share of eligible people are enrolled — there is no enrolment to measure — but what share of people who need a covered product received it without a co-payment, and for the special-authorization drugs, what share of those who need them clear the authorization step. That is a measure of access, and it is the measure the program's success should be judged on.

What can be said with confidence is narrower than the question asks. The program's reach is bounded by its covered categories: contraception and diabetes products, with rare-disease funding committed separately under section 5 [3][1]. A low national claim count is therefore not evidence of failure and a high one is not evidence of a broad program; both are consistent with a program that covers two categories and is doing what it was designed to do. Anyone citing a national "number of people using pharmacare" should be asked which jurisdictions it includes, which covered products it counts, whether special-authorization claims are included, and what date its coverage starts from.

The usage numbers themselves are not in this report. Searches for Health Canada's bilateral-agreement announcements, provincial pharmacare reporting and claims statistics returned service errors, and the page-read allowance was exhausted before any of them could be opened, so the claims and dispensing figures that Health Canada and participating provinces publish were not checked against a page. That material exists and is where this section should be rebuilt from: each bilateral agreement announcement states the federal contribution and the covered products, and participating provinces report their own dispensing. What can be said without it is the method: the program has no enrolment count by design, usage must be read from claims and dispensing by jurisdiction, and special-authorization claims must be counted separately from automatic ones. This is the largest single gap in the report, and it is flagged again under Open questions.

### 5. What the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost, and why the estimates differ

The one thing that can be established from the statute is that the Act itself contains no cost figure at all. Section 5 commits the federal government to maintaining long-term funding for the provinces, territories and Indigenous peoples to improve the accessibility and affordability of pharmaceutical products, beginning with those for rare diseases, and states that funding for provinces and territories must be provided primarily through agreements with their respective governments; it names no amount [1]. Section 6 conditions payments on agreements without stating their size [1]. There is no appropriation, no reference level and no schedule in the text. Every number in public circulation — the Parliamentary Budget Officer's costings, the government's announced envelope, the various academic and industry estimates of universal pharmacare — is an estimate of a program the Act authorises but does not fund at a stated amount. That distinction is not pedantry: it means the cost of "the full program" is a modelling question with a defensible range, not a budget line that can be looked up.

This section was meant to set out the PBO's costings and the other independent estimates, with their figures, base years, assumptions and the reasons they diverge. It does not. The PBO's universal single-payer costing, its first-phase costing and the federal government's announced envelope are all published documents, and targeted searches for them returned service errors while the page-read allowance ran out before any PBO publication could be opened. No figure in this section has therefore been checked against a primary page, and reproducing numbers from memory would put unchecked figures into a record built to be checked. What follows is the structure a proper comparison needs, not the comparison. This is the second major gap in the report, alongside the agreement list, and both are the first things a revision should close.

The reason the missing comparison matters is that pharmacare cost estimates are not measurements of one quantity. They differ because they are answers to different questions, and the differences are systematic enough to be predicted in advance. A costing of universal single-payer pharmacare has to settle at least six things before it produces a number, and each choice moves the total by billions.

The first is scope: which drugs are in. A plan covering the essential medicines list contemplated by section 8(1) of the Act is a very different proposition from a plan covering all prescription drugs, and section 8(1) asks only for a list of essential prescription drugs to inform a national formulary, not for a comprehensive one [1]. Second is the treatment of existing coverage: gross versus net. A gross figure counts all spending on covered drugs; a net figure subtracts what provincial plans, private insurers and patients already pay, and asks what the incremental public cost would be. Net costings that assume private coverage is displaced produce much lower federal numbers than gross costings, and the choice between them is a policy assumption, not a fact. Third is the payment basis: list price versus actual transaction price after negotiated rebates and generic substitution. A costing built on list prices is measuring a different quantity from one built on the prices a single payer would negotiate, and the difference is a policy assumption about bargaining power rather than an observed price.

Fourth is the delivery infrastructure — dispensing fees, wholesale markups, and whether pharmacy remuneration is included in the envelope or held constant. A costing that includes pharmacy remuneration is measuring something different from one that treats dispensing as unchanged, and the two are not always distinguished in a headline total. Fifth is the population and time frame: a costing in a given base year, held flat, versus one projected forward with population aging, drug price inflation and the arrival of new therapies. This matters more than usual here because the two categories the Act funds today are a narrow slice of prescription spending, so the gap between a first-phase costing and a full-universal costing is driven almost entirely by products the first phase does not cover. Sixth is the rare-disease commitment in section 5, which the Act places at the start of its long-term funding commitment rather than inside the section 6 categories [1]; whether a costing includes it, and at what level, is a definitional choice that changes the total.

Because these six choices are independent, two estimates can both be correct and differ by a wide margin. A comparison of PBO and other estimates is therefore only meaningful if it lines up scope, gross versus net, price basis, remuneration treatment, time frame and rare-disease treatment side by side, and states which assumption drives the difference. That table is what this section should contain, and it does not.

One point of interpretation is worth recording even without the numbers. The first phase funded by section 6 is not a scaled-down version of the universal program in the sense of being the same thing with a smaller budget. It is a different instrument: two clinical categories, first-dollar coverage, delivered through existing provincial plans, with the item-level list set in the agreements rather than in the statute [3]. Costings of universal single-payer pharmacare therefore do not describe the cost trajectory of what has actually been built, and the cost of the first phase should not be read as an early instalment whose remainder is already known. The relationship between the two depends entirely on whether the program is extended category by category or replaced by a comprehensive plan, and the Act commits to neither.


## Beyond this question

Three things follow for anyone writing about pharmacare in Canada, and they apply whether or not the numbers in this report are ever filled in.

Read the Act before the announcement. The gap between what the Pharmacare Act does — a conditional spending power over two clinical categories, delivered through provincial plans, at a first-dollar standard — and how it is described in political communication is wide, and most of the confusion in the public argument comes from that gap. A claim that Canada "has pharmacare" and a claim that Canada "has no pharmacare" can both be defended only because the Act is a framework and the coverage is a set of agreements. Anyone writing about it should say which of the two they mean.

Treat participation as the unit of analysis. Because section 6(1) gates payment on an agreement, there is no national program to describe in the singular. The honest unit is the jurisdiction: what it signed, when coverage began, which products are on its list, how many claims it has paid. A national aggregate is a sum of decisions that were made separately for different reasons, and reporting it as a program statistic hides exactly the variation that determines whether a patient pays at the counter.

Watch the special-authorization line. The distinction between automatic coverage and coverage available on application is where a first-dollar program can quietly become a partial one. Saxagliptin and metformin in the diabetes category are the documented example [2]; whether the list of such products grows is a decision made in agreements and guidance rather than in the Act, and it is not something a patient or a reporter would notice from a press release.

## Open questions

The two largest questions this report was asked are not answered in it, and both are unanswered for the same reason: the documents exist, but no page was read. Every web search run returned a service error and the page-read allowance was exhausted, so nothing from Health Canada, the Parliamentary Budget Officer, the Canadian Institute for Health Information or any provincial plan was checked against a source.

The agreement list is the first. Which provinces and territories have signed bilateral agreements, on what dates, for what federal contribution, with what covered list and what effective date, and which governments have not signed — none of this is established here. The structural facts are established: payment is conditional on an agreement [1], the item-level list is set outside the statute [3], and eligibility runs through the provincial health plan with no application process [2]. The list itself is not. A revision should build a table with one row per jurisdiction from the agreement texts, and should treat a non-signing province as a finding in its own right.

The cost figures are the second. No PBO figure, no alternative independent estimate and no announced federal envelope appears in this report. The section on cost therefore sets out the six assumptions that make pharmacare estimates diverge — scope of the covered list, gross versus net of existing coverage, list versus negotiated price, treatment of pharmacy remuneration, time frame, and whether the rare-disease commitment is inside the total [1] — without applying them to any published number. That is a method for a comparison, not the comparison.

Usage is the third and least tractable. Even with the published material in hand, Canada has no count of people enrolled in pharmacare, because there is nothing to enrol in: eligibility is automatic for residents who qualify for their provincial health plan [2]. The measurable quantity is claims paid by jurisdiction, split between automatically covered and special-authorization products, and it does not by itself show whether more people obtained a contraceptive or a diabetes product or the same people obtained it with a different payer. Whether any government has published a before-and-after dispensing analysis that separates those two effects is a question I did not answer.

Two further gaps are narrower. The item-level covered lists, and any differences between agreements, are not set out here. And the three statutory deliverables that fell due on 10 October 2025 — the Canadian Drug Agency's essential medicines list under section 8(1), the pan-Canadian appropriate-use strategy under section 10(1), and the expert committee's report on operation and financing under section 11(1) [1] — were required by dates that have passed, but whether each was delivered, published or tabled is not established in this report. Their status is checkable and matters: the essential medicines list is the document that would define the scope any future universal plan covers, and the committee's report is the one the Act requires to be tabled in Parliament.

report.title: School smartphone bans: what jurisdictions have done, what evaluations measured, and how strong the evidence is
report.body:
## TL;DR

_(to write)_

## Key Findings

_(to write)_

## Details

### 1. 1. Which jurisdictions have restricted smartphones in schools, and what do the rules actually require?

Two jurisdictions can be described precisely from their own legal instruments, and they illustrate how differently a "ban" can be written. Ontario and England both restrict phones, and neither requires phones to be locked away.

**Ontario.** The province amended its provincial Code of Conduct, with the new rules taking effect 1 September 2024, and requires every school board to have an enforcement policy and to send annual reminders to parents [5]. The rule is graded by age. For grades 7 to 12, "students’ personal mobile devices are stored out of view and powered off or set to silent mode during instructional time, except when their use is explicitly permitted by the educator under the circumstances outlined above" [1]. For grade 6 and below, the restriction runs for the whole school day rather than instructional time, and the parent-facing page states that "Students Grade 6 and below may not use cellphones or other mobile devices at school during the school day without the permission of a teacher" [5].

The enforcement mechanism is specific and deliberately low-tech. Students keep their devices: the province tells them they may keep the phone, tablet or smart watch with them, but must turn it off or set it to silent and store it out of view, "for example, in a bag or pocket" [5]. If a teacher sees a device that is not stored out of view, "they must require the device be handed in for the instructional period and the device must be placed, by the student, in a storage area in a location in the classroom designated by the educator" [1]; the parent-facing version says the device is handed in "for the class (Grades 7-12) or for the day (Grades k-6)" [5]. Escalation runs to the principal and, in the provincial policy, up to suspension for repeated non-compliance [1].

Ontario's policy also reaches beyond the handset to the network. Boards are required to "restrict access to all social media platforms on school networks and school devices." Use is permitted only for educator-directed educational purposes [1]. That is a materially different intervention from a classroom phone rule: it governs what the school's own infrastructure will serve, regardless of whether a student's phone is in a bag.

**England.** The Department for Education's guidance is statutory guidance to schools and trusts, and it is broader in time than Ontario's classroom rule: it covers a policy "that prohibits the use of mobile phones throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [6]. The default is stated flatly: "All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only" [6].

Two features of the English design matter for reading the evaluations later. First, the mechanism is devolved: "There are a number of ways in which schools can ensure that they are mobile phone-free, and it is for headteachers to decide how best to achieve this within their own unique contexts" [6] — some schools use lockers, some collect phones at the start of the day. A study of "English schools with phone bans" is therefore a study of a heterogeneous set of practices, not one treatment. Second, the guidance carries legal exceptions that override the ban: "Allowing a disabled pupil access to their mobile phone during the school day, where it is necessary due to the nature of their disability, may be considered a reasonable adjustment and a failure to do so may be a breach of the school’s duty" [6]. Medical devices such as glucose monitors fall on the same side. The English rule is thus a default prohibition with a statutory equality carve-out, not an absolute one.

The two cases already show why cross-jurisdiction comparison is treacherous. Ontario restricts during instructional time for secondary pupils and all day for younger ones, allows phones to stay in pockets, and separately blocks social media on school networks. England prohibits use across the whole day including breaks, but leaves the storage method to each headteacher. A finding from one does not transfer to the other without asking which of these features is doing the work.

*Inference:* the design differences are not administrative detail. If the hypothesised mechanism is distraction during lessons, Ontario's classroom-time rule targets it directly and England's breaktime prohibition does not. If the hypothesised mechanism is the total dose of social-media exposure across the day, England's whole-day rule and Ontario's network block are the relevant levers. Almost none of the evaluations discussed below specify which mechanism they are testing, which is the root of the interpretive problem.

### 2. 2. What have evaluations measured about learning and academic attainment?

The attainment literature is small, and its most-cited result and its most direct replication point in opposite directions.

**The English result that launched the policy wave.** Beland and Murphy's 2015 CEP discussion paper is the study that politicians cite. It surveyed schools in four English cities about their mobile phone policies and combined the responses with administrative exam data, using a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits "variations in schools’ autonomous decisions to ban these devices, conditioning on a range of student characteristics and prior achievement" [4]. The headline finding is that "student performance in high stakes exams significantly increases post ban" [4], with the gains driven by the lowest-achieving students. In the terms the authors used, the impact for low-achieving students was equivalent to "an additional hour a week in school or five additional school days a year" [3].

That effect size is modest but not trivial — a few days of extra schooling per year, concentrated on the pupils furthest behind. It is also the kind of result that invites replication, because the identifying assumption is strong: schools that chose to ban phones may have been on a different trajectory for reasons unrelated to phones, and the paper's controls can only do so much.

**The Swedish replication that found nothing.** Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors (2020) ran the test on a much larger scale: 1,086 schools in Sweden. As summarised in a 2024 review, Kessel et al. reported no improvement in student performance in schools with a phone ban, and taking into account "the timing of the ban, urban versus non-urban school setting, and socioeconomic status did not affect the pattern of results" [3].

This is the central disagreement in the attainment literature, and it is not a dispute about statistics. Two well-powered designs on administrative exam data, in two countries with similar high-stakes testing regimes, reached different conclusions. The plausible reconciliations are all untested: that English schools banning phones early were unusually motivated or unusually disordered; that Swedish bans were weaker in practice; that the English sample's gains reflect a subset of low achievers large enough to move a mean in a smaller sample but diluted in a Swedish sample of over a thousand schools; or that the English result is a specification artefact. On the record as it stands, the Swedish null is the more credible estimate of a general effect, because it is larger, later, and pre-specified against a published target. *Inference:* the English estimate should be treated as a hypothesis that failed its first large replication, not as an established effect.

**Spain: association without identification.** Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella studied bans introduced in two Spanish regions in 2015 using PISA data from 2006 to 2018. The authors' own summary is that "Although the limitations of PISA data prevented conclusive findings, children's phone use was negatively associated with schools' academic results" [3]. That is the weakest form of evidence in the set: a cross-sectional association between phone use and results, with the policy variation too coarse to identify a ban effect. It is often cited as supporting bans; it does not.

**South Australia: a preregistered test of a real state mandate.** The strongest-designed evaluation of an actual statewide ban is King and colleagues' study of South Australia's 2023 state-mandated phone ban, a preregistered controlled pre-post natural experiment across five public secondary schools. Its attainment-adjacent outcome was academic engagement, and the result was null: "Linear mixed models indicated that ban and no ban school groups did not differ significantly in terms of problematic phone use, academic engagement, and school belonging" [3]. The authors' verdict is unambiguous: "Although these results indicate limited to no short-term benefits of the ban, further evaluation with more sensitive methodologies is recommended" [3].

Two things should be said about that null in fairness. First, academic engagement is a self-report proxy, not a test score; the study was not designed to detect attainment effects and could not have. Second, a null over a short follow-up cannot rule out effects that accumulate. But the study was preregistered and controlled, and it is the closest thing in the literature to a clean test of a mandated ban in the schools that actually experienced it — and it found no engagement difference.

**What the attainment evidence amounts to.** One influential positive result from 2015 English administrative data, one large Swedish replication finding nothing, one inconclusive Spanish association, and one preregistered Australian natural experiment finding no difference in engagement. The honest summary is that no jurisdiction has demonstrated, in a design capable of supporting it, that banning phones raises attainment. The one mechanism with any support — gains concentrated among low achievers — remains a single-country finding awaiting a second confirmation.

### 3. 3. What have evaluations measured about attention, distraction and classroom climate?

Distraction is the mechanism everyone assumes and almost nobody measures. The policy case rests on the claim that phones fragment attention in class; the evaluations in this set mostly measured other things.

**The flagship study never measured attention.** Beland and Murphy's 2015 paper — the source of nearly every "phones cost you a week of school" headline — is explicit about its outcome: "This paper investigates the impact of schools banning mobile phones on student test scores" [4]. The theoretical mechanism is distraction, but the measured variable is performance on high-stakes exams. Nothing in the design observes what students did in lessons, how often they were off task, or whether the ban changed the classroom's attentional climate. The inference from exam scores back to attention is exactly that: an inference.

**The direct measure that exists is a self-report proxy, and it is null.** King and colleagues' South Australian natural experiment is the only study here that tried to measure something attention-adjacent. Its outcome was academic engagement — a self-reported construct, not observed behaviour — and the result was no difference between ban and no-ban schools: "Linear mixed models indicated that ban and no ban school groups did not differ significantly in terms of problematic phone use, academic engagement, and school belonging" [3]. Problematic phone use, likewise self-reported, also did not differ. If the ban had meaningfully reduced in-school phone use, this is the measure where it should have appeared.

**The one classroom-climate measure points the other way.** The Dutch EPoSS study (24 secondary schools, 1,398 adolescents, nine partial bans and fifteen full bans) is the only study in the set with a relational measure of the classroom: "full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging" [8]. Classroom climate is not the same as attention, but connectedness to teachers is one of the strongest correlates of engagement in the broader education literature, and it is the direction opposite to what ban advocates predict. The design is cross-sectional, so causation is unresolved — schools that escalate to full bans may already have more conflict over phones. But the result is the only direct test of the "calmer classroom" claim, and it does not support it.

**What is missing is the measurement technology.** None of these studies used the methods that would actually answer the attention question: structured classroom observation with time-sampled off-task behaviour, teacher logbooks of lesson interruptions, or device-level telemetry showing how often phones were actually out. Compliance — the single most important mediating variable — is unmeasured in every study in this set. A ban that most students ignore is not a test of banning; it is a test of announcing. The South Australian authors concede the point themselves in recommending "further evaluation with more sensitive methodologies" [3].

*Inference:* the attention literature is not "mixed" in the way the attainment literature is. It is largely absent. What exists is a theorised mechanism (phones distract), a policy response built on that theory, and two self-report measures plus one relational measure, none of which shows the predicted benefit. That is a different situation from "the evidence conflicts" — it is closer to "the evidence has not been collected."

There is a second, subtler problem with how attention is framed in the policy debate. The laboratory literature on phone presence and cognitive load is not the same as the classroom literature, and results from one do not carry to the other. A student who cannot see a phone in a bag is in a different condition from a student who can see it on the desk, and both differ from a student who is using it. Because none of these evaluations recorded where phones actually were during lessons — pocket, bag, locker, collected at the door — they cannot distinguish these conditions. The English guidance, which explicitly leaves the storage method to headteachers [6], guarantees that the treatment varies across schools in ways no study has yet captured. *Inference:* until storage conditions and compliance are recorded, the attention question cannot be answered even in principle, and the nulls should be read as nulls about the average of a heterogeneous and largely unmeasured set of practices.

One further point on interpretation. A null on self-reported academic engagement does not mean students were equally attentive; it means the two groups reported similar engagement. Self-report is vulnerable to reference-group effects — students in ban schools may rate their own engagement against a changed classroom norm. Without observational data, the direction of any such bias is unknown. This is a reason to want better measurement, not a reason to discount the null.

### 4. 4. What have evaluations measured about bullying, wellbeing and mental health?

This is where the policy case is strongest rhetorically and weakest empirically. Three recent studies — in Iceland, South Australia and the Netherlands — tested bans against wellbeing, bullying and mental-health outcomes, and all three found nothing, or found harm to the social relationships schools are trying to protect.

**Iceland: a population-scale difference-in-differences.** The most statistically powerful test is a repeated cross-sectional study of 70 Icelandic schools and 23,938 adolescent observations, comparing 2016 and 2018 (pre-policy) with 2023 (post-policy), in which 22 of the 70 schools adopted bans. Published in JAMA Network Open on 27 October 2026, it found that "schoolwide mobile phone bans were not associated with meaningful changes in depressive symptoms" [7] — and the same held for anxiety, hostility and mental wellbeing [7].

The secondary outcomes were no better for the policy. "Results were similar in gender-stratified analyses and for the secondary outcomes" — perceived peer support, screen use, in-person bullying and cyberbullying — and "Sensitivity analyses examining timing of implementation and more stringent phone restriction criteria were consistent with the main findings" [7]. The authors' conclusion is direct: "These findings suggest that school phone bans implemented in isolation may be insufficient to improve adolescent mental health at the population level" [7].

Two features make this study hard to dismiss. The sample is large enough that a policy with a real population-level effect on depressive symptoms should have shown something. And the authors tested whether stricter bans did better — the obvious objection to a null — and found that stricter bans did not. The "implemented in isolation" caveat is the honest escape hatch for advocates: a ban plus a broader mental-health or digital-literacy programme might work where a ban alone does not. But that is a hypothesis, not a finding.

**South Australia: preregistered, controlled, and null on belonging.** King and colleagues' preregistered natural experiment (five public secondary schools, 1,282 students at baseline and 1,256 at follow-up, grades 7–12, Flinders University) tested school belonging, problematic phone use, bullying, psychological distress and life satisfaction. The primary results were null across the board: "Linear mixed models indicated that ban and no ban school groups did not differ significantly in terms of problematic phone use, academic engagement, and school belonging. There was slightly higher bullying in the ban group but bullying decreased significantly in both groups" [3].

The bullying detail is worth stating precisely because it is easy to misreport. The ban schools started with slightly more bullying, and bullying fell significantly in both groups, with no ban-by-time interaction. So the honest reading is: bullying declined over the study period in both groups, and the ban did not add anything to that decline [3]. It is not evidence that bans increase bullying.

The mental-health moderators were also tested and also null: "these analyses showed that there were no significant main effects of condition or condition × time interactions on psychological distress and life satisfaction" [3]. That matters for the strongest version of the advocacy claim — that bans specifically help the vulnerable students who are struggling most. In this sample, bans did not differentially help students with poorer mental health.

**The Netherlands: full bans no better than partial, and worse for connection.** The most recent and most policy-relevant comparison comes from the Dutch EPoSS Study, reported by Vanluydt and colleagues in the Journal of Youth and Adolescence in March 2026: 1,398 adolescents with a mean age of 16.2 across 24 Dutch secondary schools, nine with partial bans and fifteen with full bans. The finding: "No significant differences were found for any of the well-being or bullying outcomes. However, full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging" [8].

This is the one result in the literature that points at a cost rather than merely an absence of benefit. It is observational and cross-sectional in design, so it cannot establish that stricter bans caused the weaker relationships — schools that adopt full bans may differ systematically from schools that do not, and it is plausible that schools with more conflict over phones are the ones that escalate to full bans. *Inference:* the association should be treated as a warning to be tested, not a demonstrated harm. But it does undercut the assumption behind escalating policy: that a stricter ban is a stronger version of the same intervention. On this evidence, stricter is not stronger; it may be different in kind.

**Why the wellbeing nulls are less surprising than they look.** School phone bans regulate a few hours of a day. Adolescents' total screen exposure, sleep timing, family environment and peer dynamics sit mostly outside school hours and outside school control. A ban that reduces in-school phone use by some amount — and compliance is unmeasured in all three studies — would be expected to move population-level depressive symptoms only if in-school use were a large share of the causal dose. The Icelandic authors' own framing — that bans implemented in isolation may be insufficient — concedes exactly this arithmetic [7].

**Bullying deserves a separate caution.** The intuition that phones enable cyberbullying is sound, and it is the reason bans are popular with parents. But cyberbullying is not confined to school hours or school networks, and the two studies that measured bullying outcomes found no ban effect [7][3]. No study in this set measured a displacement effect — whether in-school bullying fell while out-of-school messaging-based bullying rose. That is a genuine hole in the evidence rather than a null result.

### 5. 5. How strong is the evidence — designs, compliance, selection and the live disagreement among researchers?

The evidence base is small, recent, and dominated by natural experiments in which schools or states chose their own policy. The evaluations are better than the policy debate assumes and weaker than the confident claims on either side.

**The design inventory.** Six studies carry the weight. Beland and Murphy (2015) used difference-in-differences on administrative exam data with school-chosen bans in four English cities [4]. Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors (2020) applied the same logic to 1,086 Swedish schools and found nothing [3]. Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella used PISA data on two Spanish regions and could not reach conclusive findings [3]. King and colleagues ran a preregistered controlled pre-post natural experiment on South Australia's 2023 statewide ban across five public secondary schools [3]. The Icelandic study is a repeated cross-sectional difference-in-differences across 70 schools and 23,938 adolescent observations, with 22 schools adopting bans [7]. The Dutch EPoSS study is a cross-sectional comparison of nine partial-ban and fifteen full-ban schools, 1,398 adolescents [8].

Only one of the six — South Australia — was preregistered, and only that one was designed as a controlled test of a specific mandate. The two strongest nulls (Iceland and South Australia) were published in 2026; the positive result everyone cites is from 2015. That sequencing is itself informative: as designs improved and samples grew, the effects shrank toward zero.

**Problem one: the treatment is not one thing.** "A phone ban" covers rules that differ in when they apply, where the phone physically goes, and what backs them up. Ontario restricts secondary pupils during instructional time, lets them keep phones in a pocket, and separately blocks social media on school networks [1][5]. England prohibits use across the whole day including breaks, but states that "it is for headteachers to decide how best to achieve this within their own unique contexts" [6], and carves out statutory exceptions for disabled pupils [6]. The Netherlands study distinguishes partial from full bans and finds they behave differently [8]. Pooling these as one intervention is a category error, and the meta-analytic instinct to average them would produce a number that describes nothing.

**Problem two: selection.** Schools and states do not adopt bans at random. Beland and Murphy's identification rests on "variations in schools’ autonomous decisions to ban these devices" [4] — precisely the variation most likely to correlate with a school's culture, leadership and prior trajectory. The Swedish design inherits the same problem. The Dutch study is cross-sectional and cannot rule out that schools with more phone conflict escalate to full bans, which would make the connectedness finding an artefact of school type rather than a consequence of policy [8]. King and colleagues are explicit about the limit in their own work: "this study did not employ a fully randomized school selection and sample allocation protocol; therefore, the study sample should not be considered representative" [2].

**Problem three: statistical power and attrition.** The South Australian study is small: "A total of 1,282 students returned the baseline survey, and 1,256 students returned the second survey (NB: 1,338 students returned at least one survey and 597 students returned both surveys)" [2]. The repeated-measures analysis therefore rests on 597 students out of 1,338 — a minority of the sample, and one selected by whether they were present and willing at both waves. Against that, the Icelandic study is large enough that a population-level effect on depressive symptoms should have been detectable, and its authors tested stricter-ban subgroups without finding anything [7]. Power is a real limitation of the Australian study and a weak objection to the Icelandic one.

**Problem four: outcomes are proxies, and the proxies are self-report.** Academic engagement, school belonging, problematic phone use, peer support and bullying were all measured by questionnaire. Only Beland and Murphy and Kessel used administrative attainment data, and only Beland and Murphy found an effect. No study in this set measured observed classroom behaviour, device telemetry, or compliance. The gap between what the policy claims to change (attention in lessons) and what the studies measure (self-reported engagement and wellbeing) is the largest single weakness in the field.

**Problem five: follow-up is short.** South Australia's evaluation covers the period immediately after a 2023 mandate. Attainment effects, if they exist, accumulate over years of schooling. A short null is a null about short-run effects and cannot exclude a slow-building benefit — though it is worth noting that the same logic would excuse almost any null, which is why the burden should sit with the claim rather than the absence of one.

**The live disagreement.** The substantive dispute is between the Beland-Murphy result and the Kessel replication. The 2024 review literature summarising both notes that the field is "small but mixed" and that differences in context, methodology and the nature of the ban complicate synthesis [2]. There is no published reconciliation: nobody has shown that the English schools were unusual, that Swedish bans were weaker in practice, or that one specification is wrong. The most defensible reading on current evidence is that the Swedish null is the better estimate of a general effect, because it is larger, later, and tests a published finding rather than generating one.

The second disagreement is between the "bans alone" position and the compound-intervention position. The Icelandic authors conclude that bans "implemented in isolation may be insufficient to improve adolescent mental health at the population level" [7] — which is an invitation to test bans bundled with digital-literacy curricula, parent engagement or mental-health support. No such bundled evaluation exists in this set. The claim is plausible and untested, and it should not be reported as if the nulls had been overturned.

**What would move the evidence.** Three designs, none of which has been run. First, registry-linked attainment with staggered state adoption and recorded compliance, so that the dose of the intervention is measured rather than assumed. Second, within-school randomisation of storage condition (collected at the door versus pocket versus locker) with observed off-task sampling — this is the only design that isolates the mechanism the policy claims. Third, a displacement study measuring in-school and out-of-school bullying simultaneously, since the cyberbullying rationale has never been tested for substitution. Until at least the first of these exists, the honest verdict is that school phone bans are a plausible, popular, and unevaluated intervention whose best-designed tests have so far returned nulls.
